title: Big Ten expands live replay look-in to most home games, days after Michigan controversy
content:
The Big Ten will expand its live instant replay look-in to all conference home games officiated by Big Ten referees, the league announced Wednesday, allowing fans to listen and watch the replay discussion as it happens.

The move comes after days of backlash toward the Big Ten for Michigan’s last-second Hail Mary win over Western Michigan. Replay review put one second back on the clock based on the league’s own replay camera feed of the clock, rather than one used by NBC. The Big Ten released video and audio of the discussion two hours after the game ended.

The ACC first added live replay look-in for select games last season. The Big Ten and Big 12 joined this year, with the Big Ten adding it only for Friday games with Big Ten officials. Now, that expands to most Big Ten home games. It will not include this weekend’s Oklahoma-Michigan game, which will have SEC officials. The SEC is the only Power 4 conference without live replay look-in.

The Mid-American Conference on Tuesday argued in a statement that Big Ten officials did not follow proper protocol and that the TV program feed with the superimposed clock, which had expired, should have been used. The NCAA football rulebook allows a separate clock feed for replay, but that feed must also be available on TV. It’s unclear if NBC had access to the feed the Big Ten used to determine one second remained. The network did not respond to a request for clarification.

The NCAA’s rules editor issued a protocol clarification Tuesday, saying that the TV program feed with the superimposed clock should be used by everyone in that situation. It was already the baseline for every other conference, but the Big Ten uses a separate Hawk-Eye technology to sync cameras and replay.

The MAC asked the FBS Oversight Committee and the College Football Playoff to overturn the result. The NCAA said the oversight committee did not have such power and the result was final. The Big Ten said Tuesday it stood by its statement from Saturday.

Had the public and the NBC broadcast had access to Saturday night’s replay discussion as it happened live, perhaps the ensuing conversation and drama could have been prevented. Moving forward, the public will see a lot more of those discussions in the moment.

— Scott Dochterman contributed to this report
